liturgical_day: Thursday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: Rejoice with me
theme: The sinner who returns is someone heaven has been waiting to welcome.
introduction: Sinners come close to hear Jesus, and his welcome draws complaints. He answers with two searches: a shepherd goes after a lost sheep, and a woman searches her house for a missing coin. Both end with an invitation to share the finder's joy. The Fathers hear Christ's mercy in the shepherd's care and recognize God's image in the recovered coin. They also take penance seriously. Being found means turning from the sins that carried us away.
hero_alt: A shepherd carries a recovered sheep on his shoulders beneath a gold sky; a woman searches for a silver coin by candlelight in an adjoining house, in Byzantine mosaic and stained glass.
closing: The shepherd asks his friends to rejoice with him. Gregory notices that the joy belongs to the one who searched: our restored life is Christ's joy. That leaves us with something to examine. When someone turns back to God, do we welcome the return or keep rehearsing the fault? And where we ourselves have wandered, Gregory calls for a penance that changes what we do, rather than tears followed by the same wrong.

verses.text: Now the publicans and sinners drew near to him to hear him.
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Ambrose sees hope for those who have fallen: the physician still has a remedy, and the judge has not refused pardon.
verses.commentary: Ambrose connects the arrival of the publicans with the teaching that came before it. The hearer has been warned against putting passing possessions before eternal things. Yet human weakness makes a steady course difficult, and people do fall. Christ does not leave the fallen without help. Ambrose calls him both a good physician, who provides a remedy after the injury, and a merciful judge, who leaves open the hope of pardon. The sinners approaching Jesus show where that hope can bring them: within hearing of the one who can heal.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: And the Pharisees and the scribes murmured, saying: This man receives sinners and eats with them.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory distinguishes loving correction from contempt. Genuine righteousness can rebuke a fault while remaining humble before the person who has fallen.
verses.commentary: Gregory contrasts the compassion of true righteousness with the scorn of a righteousness that is only apparent. A just person may need to correct someone firmly, but charity remains within the correction. Such a person inwardly places the one being corrected above himself, so that discipline does not destroy humility. Pride works differently. It looks down on everyone else and refuses to stoop toward weakness. Gregory sees that pride in the complaint against Jesus: the accusers condemn mercy while failing to recognize how badly they need healing themselves.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: And he spoke this parable to them, saying:
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Christ answers people who do not know they are sick with a familiar story. His reply is itself an act of healing.
verses.commentary: Gregory describes the Pharisees as sick people who have not recognized their illness. Christ therefore answers them as a heavenly physician, choosing a gentle treatment rather than answering their contempt with contempt. The parable begins with an experience they can recognize in ordinary human life. A person searches for something that belongs to him and has gone missing. Through that familiar concern, Christ leads his hearers toward the mercy of their Creator. The story is addressed to the accusers because they too need to learn what their own condition is.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: What man among you who has a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the desert and go after the one that was lost until he finds it?
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril reads the flock as the creatures under Christ's care. Seeking the lost does not mean abandoning those already safe.
verses.commentary: Cyril reads the hundred sheep as a figure of the full company of rational creatures subject to the Saviour. The wandering sheep is the human race on earth. He then raises an objection: does the shepherd care for the one because he has become angry with the others? Certainly not. Those who remain are safe under the protection of the Almighty. Mercy turns toward the one in danger so that the flock may be whole again. The search expresses care for what is missing without withdrawing care from what is already secure.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: And when he has found it, does he not lay it on his shoulders, rejoicing,
verses.author: St Gregory of Nyssa
verses.insight: The shepherd carries the sheep gently. Gregory notices that the recovery comes through care, without punishment or driving the sheep before him.
verses.commentary: Gregory of Nyssa pauses over the way the shepherd brings the sheep back. Finding it does not lead to punishment. Nor does the shepherd force it along ahead of him until it reaches the flock. He lifts it onto his own shoulder and carries it gently. Gregory understands the manner of the return as part of the mercy the parable reveals. The sheep is reunited with the flock through the shepherd's care. His joy accompanies the burden he takes up, rather than waiting until the recovered animal has made its own way home.
verses.source_label: St Gregory of Nyssa, Homily on the Sinful Woman, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: and, coming home, call together his friends and neighbours, saying to them: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost?
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: The invitation is to rejoice with the shepherd. Gregory hears in it Christ's own joy at bringing humanity home.
verses.commentary: Gregory reads the shepherd's homecoming as Christ's return to his heavenly kingdom after restoring humanity. The friends and neighbours are the angels: they do his will faithfully and remain near him in the vision of his brightness. Gregory then draws attention to the invitation itself. The shepherd asks them to rejoice with him, rather than simply with the recovered sheep. Our life is a cause of joy to the Saviour. When those who were lost are brought home to heaven, their return belongs to the gladness he shares with the heavenly company.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: I say to you that, even so, there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who does penance, more than over ninety-nine just people who need no penance.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Remembered sins can stir a penitent to fervent love. Gregory also insists that this does not make sin preferable to a faithful, humble life.
verses.commentary: Gregory explains that someone conscious of former sins may turn toward God with an urgency that a complacent person lacks. Grief over having wandered can awaken love and lead to good works that make up for earlier losses. He compares this to a soldier who returns from flight and then fights bravely. But Gregory immediately guards against a false conclusion. Many just people bring such joy by their lives that no sinner's penance is to be preferred to them. The comparison challenges sluggish confidence; it does not diminish humble and faithful holiness.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:1–7

verses.text: Or what woman who has ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a candle, sweep the house, and search diligently until she finds it?
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory sees the lost coin as humanity bearing God's image. The candle points to divine wisdom appearing in the flesh to recover that likeness.
verses.commentary: Gregory understands the woman, like the shepherd, as a figure of God seeking humanity. The coin bears an image; its loss points to the way sin takes a human being away from the likeness of the Creator. The lighted candle is divine wisdom made visible in human flesh, as light shines within an earthen vessel. Its light unsettles the conscience. Gregory links this disturbance with the sweeping of the house: the mind must be shaken from its faults so that it may be cleansed and the Creator's likeness restored.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:8–10

verses.text: And when she has found it, does she not call together her friends and neighbours, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found the coin which I had lost?
verses.author: St Gregory Nazianzen
verses.insight: The heavenly powers share the joy of recovery. Gregory connects their rejoicing with their service in God's saving work.
verses.commentary: Gregory Nazianzen identifies the friends invited to celebrate with the heavenly powers. God has made them servants of his saving work, and he also gives them a share in its joy. The recovery of the lost coin therefore does not end in a private satisfaction that remains with the finder alone. Those who serve God's purposes are invited to rejoice at their fulfilment. Gregory's brief comment connects their ministry with their gladness: the heavenly powers who take part in God's work also participate in the celebration when the lost is found.
verses.source_label: St Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 45.26, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:8–10

verses.text: So I say to you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner doing penance.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: For Gregory, penance joins sorrow for past sins to a changed life. Tears alone do not complete the return.
verses.commentary: Gregory explains repentance through what a person does after grieving over sin. It means mourning past wrongs and refusing to commit further acts that will need the same mourning. Someone who weeps over one set of sins while continuing in another has not yet learned this work, or is pretending to do it. Gregory also asks the penitent to accept restraint even in lawful things, remembering the seriousness of former offences. His point is practical and demanding: the return that brings joy to heaven must reach the conduct of the person who returns.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, Homily 34 on the Gospels, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 15:8–10
